source.title: MARTI-MARS$^2$: Scaling Multi-Agent Self-Search via Reinforcement Learning for Code Generation
source.authors: Shijie Wang; Pengfei Li; Yikun Fu; Kaifeng Liu; Fangyuan Li; Yang Liu; Xiaowei Sun; Zonglin Li; Siyao Zhao; Jian Zhao; Kai Tian; Dong Li; Junqi Gao; Yutong Zhang; Yiqun Chen; Yuqiang Li; Zoe Li; Weinan Zhang; Peng Ye; Shuyue Hu; Lei Bai; Bowen Zhou; Kaiyan Zhang; Biqing Qi

record.tranche_reason: The study reports a multi-agent scaling result for code-generation performance, but does not test held-out pretraining loss power laws, extrapolation from smaller runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results concern RL training and test-time collaboration across agents. These are a different scaling mechanism from the claim's pretraining loss laws; the reported code-performance outcomes are recorded as findings outside the listed versions. The paper also mentions published work on test-time scaling, but those cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper studies multi-agent RL training and tree-search inference for code generation on LiveCodeBench v6. It reports Pass@1, Pass@1(MCTS), Pass@N and diversity metrics. It measures no pretraining loss, fits no power law in parameters, tokens or compute, does no compute-optimal allocation and no fixed-size architecture sweep. Its 'multi-agent scaling law' is a qualitative ordering (single < homogeneous < heterogeneous agents), not a fitted scaling relation. Model sizes 8B/14B/32B are different off-the-shelf models, so the study cannot show downstream predictability with scale (V6). The finding belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors claim a 'multi-agent scaling law'. Moving from single-agent to homogeneous multi-role and then heterogeneous multi-agent RL yields higher RL performance ceilings, more robust test-time scaling and greater policy diversity. They also report two 32B models collaborating reach 77.7% on LiveCodeBench, surpassing o4-mini (high) and GPT-5.1.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates multi-agent systems on code generation; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute, or fit compute-optimal allocation curves.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary across model combinations, agent counts, training configurations, and inference budgets.

fits_no_version.finding: The paper reports an ordering on LiveCodeBench v6: single-agent GRPO, then homogeneous multi-role RL, then heterogeneous multi-agent RL give higher Pass@1/Pass@1(MCTS). Gains in Pass@K and diversity with more agents are not monotonic: in Table 3, 14B 3-model Heter 80.0 vs 2-model 81.7; in Table 9, 3-model Pass@K 0.737 vs 2-model 0.754.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-agent RL collaboration (agent count and heterogeneity) raises code-generation performance ceilings as a scaling axis separate from parameter count.

record.problems: The reported outcomes are code-generation benchmark metrics, not held-out pretraining losses. The paper does not fit or test the claim's power laws or report uncertainty estimates for the relevant results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained; the selected findings capture the paper's explicit multi-agent code-performance results relevant as an alternate scaling dimension.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no loss is measured.
Extrapolation of fitted laws to larger runs.
Depth/width effects at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities or regimes; RL post-training gains are not fitted to any power law.
Downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss; the 8B/14B/32B models differ in family and training, and no trend is fitted.
Dependence of exponents or allocations on fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: 'Scaling law' here is used loosely for a qualitative trend over agent paradigms; there is no fitted functional form. The appendix contains an unfilled placeholder ('stabilizing at a budget of XX'). No uncertainty is reported, and results come from a single benchmark. The reader's T6/discusses classification is kept.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of loss from smaller to substantially larger pretraining runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture comparisons at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from pretraining loss or conventional model/training scale; the reported scaling is by multi-agent collaboration and RL.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.measure: Pass@1 change relative to base model
rows.note: The paper also reports increases of 4.4% over Vanilla-GRPO and 2.9% over the peak Homo-MARS2 result. This is an RL-training result, not a pretraining loss scaling result.
rows.check: This is an RL-method comparison: the paper's own method against the base model. It does not measure a scaling-law effect. The value is relative Pass@1 (+8.0%), which is fine as a record of the paper's claim.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B & AReaL-boba-2-8B
rows.note: The paper presents this as multi-agent code-generation performance and solution-space exploration, not as a pretraining loss scaling result.
rows.check: This is a Pass@K for the paper's own method (Table 3). It has no baseline and bears on no version. The comparable Vanilla-TTS Q-8B & A-8B value is 72.0.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B & AReaL-boba-2-14B
rows.note: The paper identifies this as the highest Pass@K in its 14B family; it does not fit or evaluate a pretraining loss power law.
rows.check: This is the paper's own method value from Table 3 and bears on no version.

rows.subject: Qwen3-14B & AReaL-boba-2-14B & DeepCoder-14B-Preview
rows.note: The reported three-model value is lower than the 81.7% two-model value in row r3, so the table does not show a monotonic increase for this comparison.
rows.check: This is the paper's own method value. The 3-model value (80.0) is below the 2-model value (81.7), so adding agents gave no monotonic gain here. The finding concerns agent count, not any scaling-law version.
